title: Firewall authentication methods
content:
## Active vs. Passive Authentication

All authentication methods—local password authentication, server-based authentication, and two-factor authentication—use active authentication. Active authentication means that users are prompted to manually enter their login credentials before being granted access.

Not all users authenticate in the same way. Some users can be granted access transparently, because user information is determined without asking the user to enter their login credentials. This is known as passive authentication. Passive authentication occurs with the single sign-on method: FSSO, RSSO, and NTLM.

![Firewall authentication methods](diagram:0)

## Two-Factor Authentication

Traditional user authentication requires your username plus something you know, such as a password. The weakness is that if someone obtains your username, they need only your password to compromise your account. Two-factor authentication requires something you know, such as a password, and something you have, such as a token or certificate. Because this method places less importance on often vulnerable passwords, it makes compromising the account more complex for an attacker.

You can use two-factor authentication on FortiGate with both user and administrator accounts. Note that you cannot use two-factor authentication with explicit proxies.

FortiGate can deliver OTPs (one-time passwords) through tokens such as FortiToken 200 (hardware token) and FortiToken Mobile (software token), as well as through email or SMS. OTPs are more secure than static passwords because the passcode changes at regular intervals and is valid for only a short amount of time. FortiTokens generate a new, six-digit password every 60 seconds by default. An NTP server is highly recommended to ensure the OTPs remain in sync.

FortiToken Mobile Push allows users to accept the authorization request from their FortiToken mobile app, without the need to enter an additional code.

Each FortiGate (and FortiGate VM) provides two free FortiToken Mobile activations. You cannot register the same FortiToken on more than one FortiGate. If you want to use the same FortiToken for authentication on multiple FortiGate devices, you must use a central validation server, such as FortiAuthenticator.

## Firewall Policies and Authentication

A firewall policy consists of access and inspection rules that tell FortiGate how to handle traffic. You can use the source of a firewall policy to control authentication. The source of a firewall policy must include the source address (IP address), but you can also include the user and user group. User and user group objects can consist of local firewall accounts, external server accounts, PKI users, and FSSO users.

Active authentication prompts the user for credentials based on the protocol of the traffic and the firewall policy. The firewall policy must specify the allowed protocols such as HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, and Telnet. If the firewall policy that has authentication enabled does not allow at least one of the supported protocols used for obtaining user credentials, the user will not be able to authenticate.

DNS is allowed through the firewall before successful user authentication because it is a base protocol. DNS must still be defined in the policy as allowed in order for it to pass. HTTP service is TCP port 80 and does not include DNS (UDP port 53).

## Authentication Behavior and Timeout

When active authentication is used with a fall-through policy that does not have authentication enabled, all traffic will use the fall-through policy, meaning users are not prompted to authenticate. You can change the `auth-on-demand` option via CLI:
- **Implicitly** (default): Will not trigger authentication if there is a fall-through policy.
- **Always**: Triggers an authentication prompt for policies that have active authentication enabled regardless of a fall-through policy. Traffic is not allowed until authentication is successful.

If you want all users on a specific interface to authenticate before accessing any resources, enable captive portal authentication at the interface level.

Authentication timeout options protect against unauthorized access:
- **Idle**: If there are no packets from the host device within the configured timeframe, the user is logged out.
- **Hard**: An absolute time value. Regardless of the user's behavior, the timer starts as soon as the user authenticates and expires after the configured value.
- **New session**: Authentication expires if no new sessions are created through the firewall from the host device within the configured timeout value.

## Monitoring Authenticated Users

You can monitor users who authenticate through your firewall policies using the Dashboard > Assets & Identities > Firewall Users page. It displays the user, user group, duration, IP address, traffic volume, and authentication method. It does not include administrators, because they are not authenticating through firewall policies. This page also allows you to disconnect a user, or multiple users, at the same time.

> **Key terms:** DNS is a base protocol; hostname resolution is almost always a requirement for any protocol to work.
